pages.title: Why this Atlas exists
pages.body_markdown:
Personal Atlas exists to hold a meaningful part of a life in one place: things written, encountered, experienced, considered, and not yet understood.

**One collection, many entrances.**

It is a commonplace book in spirit, an atlas in navigation, and a network underneath. An outline provides orientation; connections allow the same thing to belong in more than one part of life.

Life areas describe what something concerns. Entry kinds describe what it is. Connections describe what it relates to. A poem can concern travel, connect to an experience, and remain a poem without being copied into several folders.

The Atlas is comprehensive in what it can hold and undemanding in what it asks. Making and appreciating have separate entrances. Play has room outside achievement. A feeling does not have to become a lesson, and an interest does not have to become a project.

This is not a report card or a compulsory diary. It can add context alongside existing tools rather than replace them. Its organization can change as its owner changes.

pages.title: Influences and departures
pages.body_markdown:
## Influences, not instructions

### Michel Foucault: collecting and returning

In “Self Writing,” Foucault discusses *hupomnemata*: notebooks that gather material encountered through reading, listening, and thought for later use and reflection. He distinguishes them from confessional journals. The Atlas borrows the practice of collecting and returning, while extending it to original writing, experiences, and practical context. It does not claim to reproduce an ancient practice or adopt Foucault's wider philosophy.

### William James: different aspects of self

In *The Principles of Psychology*, Chapter X, James discusses material, social, and spiritual aspects of self within a larger account. The spiritual aspect here concerns inner capacities and dispositions, not only religion. The Atlas borrows the idea of several perspectives on a person, not a rigid three-part taxonomy or a complete account of James's theory.

### The Atlas's own adaptation

How am I living? How am I relating? What am I becoming?

These questions are this project's adaptation, not quotations from either thinker. They are optional perspectives, not categories every entry must satisfy.

A commonplace book in spirit, an atlas in navigation, and a network underneath.

The map should remain revisable. These influences can be questioned, expanded, or replaced as the notebook develops.

## References

- [Michel Foucault, “Self Writing”](https://foucault.info/documents/foucault.hypomnemata.en/)
- [William James, *The Principles of Psychology*, Chapter X](https://psychclassics.yorku.ca/James/Principles/prin10.htm)

The references require an internet connection to open. This page's text remains available offline.
